content:
Quick answer: Arthritis can affect work through pain, fatigue and changes in movement. Help may include changes to tasks, hours or equipment, an occupational health assessment and Access to Work support. Disability and flexible-working law differ between Great Britain and Northern Ireland. A diagnosis alone does not settle every legal entitlement.

Does arthritis count as a disability?

In England, Scotland and Wales, the Equality Act 2010 definition concerns an impairment with a substantial, long-term adverse effect on normal daily activities. The effect of arthritis on the person matters, not simply the condition's name. Do not assume every diagnosis automatically meets the test or that being able to work rules disability out.

Northern Ireland has a different legal framework, including the Disability Discrimination Act 1995. nidirect explains employment protections and reasonable adjustments. Use advice for the place where you work rather than assuming the Equality Act applies across the UK.

Asking for reasonable adjustments

Reasonable adjustments aim to reduce a disabled person's disadvantage at work. Acas explains the duty in Great Britain, including when an employer knows, or could reasonably be expected to know, that someone is disabled. A formal disclosure is not the only way that knowledge can arise.

What is reasonable depends on the circumstances, including whether a change would help, whether it is practical and its cost. Possible changes to discuss include:

  • Different start or finish times, planned breaks or a phased return after absence.
  • Changes to duties, workload or how a task is done.
  • Suitable equipment or changes to the workspace.
  • Access arrangements and time for relevant appointments or treatment.

These are examples for discussion, not a guarantee that every request must be agreed. An occupational therapist, physiotherapist or occupational health professional may help identify what fits your tasks and symptoms. NICE's rheumatoid arthritis guidance supports specialist occupational therapy when everyday activities or hand function are affected. That clinical guidance does not decide an employment-law dispute.

Preparing for a conversation with your manager

Explain the work task that is difficult, what happens when you try it and what change might help. A short record of pain, fatigue, time taken and better or worse days can make the discussion specific. You can ask to try an adjustment and agree a review date.

Think about whom you want involved, such as your manager, HR, occupational health or a union representative. Ask how health information will be used and who needs to see it. If you are worried about discrimination or an employment decision, get advice rather than relying on a general article to predict the outcome.

Flexible working: a request is not the same as an adjustment

In Great Britain, employees can make a statutory flexible-working request from their first day in a job. Employers must handle requests reasonably, but this is a right to request, not an automatic right to the working pattern requested.

Northern Ireland's statutory route has different qualifying rules, including a continuous-employment requirement. Check the current rules before applying. Anyone can discuss flexibility with an employer even if they do not qualify for a statutory request.

A request for a disability-related reasonable adjustment is a separate matter. Do not assume that a refusal under the general flexible-working process settles the employer's adjustment duties.

Access to Work

Access to Work in Great Britain may help with practical support such as specialist equipment, support workers or travel where its eligibility rules are met. Check eligibility for your work situation, including self-employment, before relying on support.

Access to Work does not pay for reasonable adjustments that the employer is legally responsible for. It is not a substitute for that duty or a promise that a particular item will be funded. Northern Ireland has a separate programme, signposted through nidirect's support-while-in-work guide. Check the relevant service before buying equipment or making financial commitments.

Occupational health and medical information

An occupational health assessment can help explore how your job and health affect each other, possible adjustments and a return-to-work plan. Acas explains assessment and consent. The adviser must ask permission before sharing the assessment with the employer.

Discuss what the report will contain and how it will be used. An employer must keep the information confidential and limit access to people who genuinely need it. A report may contain relevant health information as well as recommendations, so do not assume it contains no medical details.

Absence and sick pay

Ask how disability-related absence is recorded and whether the absence policy needs adjustment. Acas says review points should not automatically trigger disciplinary action. Employers should consider individual circumstances and reasonable adjustments. This does not mean every disability-related absence is automatically excluded from all procedures.

For eligible employees, Statutory Sick Pay is payable from the first full day of sickness absence under the rules introduced on 6 April 2026. The previous three waiting days no longer apply to new absences under those rules. Check eligibility, your contract and your employer's sickness-reporting procedure. Contractual sick pay may be different. Older absences spanning the change can have transitional rules.

Managing symptoms alongside work

The NHS rheumatoid arthritis living-with guide discusses self-management, work and support. Ask your healthcare team about activity, rest and ways to protect your joints that fit your condition and duties.

  • Plan demanding tasks and breaks around your ability rather than trying to make up all missed work on a better day.
  • Ask for an equipment or task assessment rather than assuming a particular chair, desk or keyboard will relieve your symptoms.
  • Keep a flare plan that explains whom to contact and what temporary changes may help.
  • Take medicines exactly as prescribed, including their timing and food instructions. Do not move every medicine to breakfast or change doses to get through a shift.

Self-employment may offer choices about scheduling, but it does not guarantee easier symptoms, stable income or entitlement to employee protections. Check the support available for your actual work status before changing hours or leaving employment.

Getting further advice

For a work problem in Great Britain, start with Acas, your union or a qualified adviser. In Northern Ireland, use the advice routes in nidirect's employment and disability guidance. Get advice promptly if a decision or deadline may affect your rights.

If you need benefits help, our benefits and PIP hub is a starting point, not a decision on eligibility. Benefits, employment rights and workplace adjustments have different rules. An online chat cannot give a binding legal decision or an individual medical assessment.
